673.title: Diwali: the row of lamps
673.hook: Ayodhya lights a lamp on every doorstep for Rama: from darkness, lead me to light
673.carry: from darkness, lead me to light
673.howItsDone: At Diwali, Hindu families clean and decorate their homes, draw rangoli at the door, light rows of clay oil lamps, worship Lakshmi on the new-moon night, share sweets and visit relatives; in many homes a small lamp is also lit at the shrine every evening at dusk.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Navaratri, nine nights of the Goddess. Your line was shakti: the divine mother is the power in all. Today, the darkest night of the month.
screen: `SHAKTI: THE DIVINE MOTHER IS THE POWER IN ALL.`

segments.voice: No moon at all. And on that night, a whole city does the opposite of sleeping. Every doorstep, every windowsill, every wall gets a small clay lamp, a little cup of oil with a cotton wick. The story many families tell their children is simple: Rama is coming home after fourteen years, and the people of Ayodhya light the way so he can find it in the dark. Valmiki's own telling doesn't mention the lamps; they're the festival's telling. Today, why they burn.
screen: `NO MOON TONIGHT.` → `A LAMP ON EVERY DOORSTEP.` → `SO HE CAN FIND HIS WAY.`

segments.voice: First, the story as families tell it. Fourteen years earlier, Rama left Ayodhya for the forest so his father could keep a promise. His brother Bharata wouldn't take the throne; he set Rama's sandals on it and ruled as their keeper, and vowed that if Rama wasn't back the day the fourteen years ran out, he'd walk into fire. So the whole city waits. In the telling children hear, Rama comes home on amavasya, the new-moon night, and so he won't miss the road, the people put a lamp on every doorstep. Deepa, lamp; avali, a row: Deepavali. Many teachers say the darkest night is the point. In Hindu teaching the deepest dark isn't outside. It's avidya, not knowing who you really are, and the light is knowing God and the self, the atman, that shines in you. One of the oldest prayers, from the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, asks for exactly that: tamaso ma jyotir gamaya. From darkness, lead me to light. Many read every Diwali lamp as that prayer, said with a flame. That's why, in many Hindu homes, a small lamp is lit at the shrine every evening at dusk, often with a short prayer to the light. Diwali is that evening lamp, lit by a whole city. And it meets a dark week of your own the same way: the tradition doesn't say cheer up. It says light one lamp, and ask to see what's true. The night is shared, too: Lakshmi is welcomed through lit doors, Jains mark Mahavira's liberation, and Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas.
screen: `BHARATA WAITS. SANDALS ON THE THRONE.` · `DEEPAVALI: A ROW OF LAMPS.` · `AVIDYA: THE DARK OF NOT KNOWING.` · `TAMASO MA JYOTIR GAMAYA.` · then, large: `FROM DARKNESS, LEAD ME TO LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Many Hindu homes light a small lamp at dusk. If it's safe, light a candle or a lamp, turn off the other lights, and look at the flame. On each slow breath out, say inwardly: tamaso ma jyotir gamaya, from darkness, lead me to light. If you don't pray, ask the question under it instead: what am I not seeing clearly yet? Stay with the flame until the sit ends.
Diwali. Deepavali, a row of lamps on the darkest night: the old prayer, from darkness lead me to light, set on every doorstep.
screen: `DIWALI — today's word`.

674.title: Holi: the festival of colors
674.hook: Prahlad walks out of the fire unharmed; the next morning everyone throws color and nobody is a stranger
674.carry: bhakti walks out of the fire
674.tomorrow: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
674.howItsDone: On the full-moon night of Phalguna, many Hindus light the Holika Dahan bonfire and circle it with offerings; the next morning they play with colored powder and water, visit friends and family, and share sweets like gujiya.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Diwali, the row of lamps on the darkest night. Your line was from darkness, lead me to light. Today, a fire the night before, and color the morning after.
screen: `FROM DARKNESS, LEAD ME TO LIGHT.`

segments.voice: In the days before Holi, in many villages and city lanes, a pile starts to grow at a crossroads or an open patch of ground: branches, scrap wood, cakes of dried cow dung, whatever people can spare. Sometimes a small figure is set on top. On the full-moon night, people gather around it at dusk, walk around it, offer grain and coconut, and then light it. Tomorrow these streets will be pink and green. Tonight belongs to the fire, and the fire has a name.
screen: `A PILE GROWS AT THE CROSSROADS.` → `LIT ON THE FULL-MOON NIGHT.` → `THE FIRE HAS A NAME.`

segments.voice: The bonfire is called Holika Dahan, the burning of Holika. The story behind it belongs to a demon king, Hiranyakashipu, who has made himself almost impossible to kill and demands to be worshiped. His own son, Prahlad, a boy, won't do it. Prahlad is devoted to Vishnu, and says so. The Bhagavata Purana tells how the king tried again and again to destroy his son, and how every attempt failed. The version Holi remembers adds the king's sister, Holika. In the story people tell, fire could not harm her, and she sits in a blazing pyre with the boy in her lap, to burn him. Instead, the fire takes her, and Prahlad walks out unharmed, still saying the name of Vishnu. That's the teaching Holi keeps alive: bhakti, loving trust in God, is safer than any power a king can hold. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says it plainly: my devotee never perishes. So the bonfire is a remembering: the pride and cruelty burned, the trusting child safe. Then comes the morning after the full moon of Phalguna, at the edge of spring, when the streets fill with gulal, colored powder, and water. Neighbors who don't speak, bosses and workers, old and young, all get the same handful of pink on the face. Many people use Holi to visit, forgive, and start again, and many read the colors through Prahlad's own teaching in the Bhagavata: the Lord lives in every being, so nobody stands above anybody else.
screen: `HOLIKA DAHAN: THE BONFIRE.` · `PRAHLAD WON'T BOW.` · `THE FIRE TAKES HOLIKA, NOT THE BOY.` · `BHAKTI: MY DEVOTEE NEVER PERISHES.` · then, large: `BHAKTI WALKS OUT OF THE FIRE.`

segments.voice: On Holika Dahan, families walk around the fire and offer grain. Sit, and on each slow breath out, say Vishnu's name as many devotees do, Om Namo Narayanaya, or, if you don't pray, the word trust. Then bring to mind one small grudge you've been carrying and picture it as a stick of wood. Lay it on the fire. You don't have to forgive anyone yet; just let your hands be empty.
Holi. A bonfire for Prahlad, the devoted child the fire couldn't take, then a spring morning of color when everyone looks the same.

675.title: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
675.hook: a night kept awake, water poured over the lingam, Om Namah Shivaya until dawn
675.tomorrow: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection
675.howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri many Hindus fast, visit Shiva temples, pour water or milk over the lingam with bilva leaves, and keep vigil through the night repeating Om Namah Shivaya; many temples stay open until dawn.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Holi, a bonfire for Prahlad and a morning of color. Your line was bhakti walks out of the fire. Today, a night nobody sleeps.
screen: `BHAKTI WALKS OUT OF THE FIRE.`

segments.voice: A hunter goes into the forest and finds nothing, all day. Night falls, and he's too far from home and too stubborn to go back empty-handed. So he climbs a tree beside a pool, where animals will come to drink, and waits. He hasn't eaten. He can't let himself sleep, or he'll fall. To keep busy, he plucks leaves off the branch, one by one, and drops them without looking where they land. This is one of the stories told on Maha Shivaratri: a man who keeps the festival perfectly without knowing it exists.
screen: `A HUNTER WITH NOTHING.` → `A TREE BESIDE A POOL.` → `LEAVES DROPPED IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Shiva-ratri: the night of Shiva, the fourteenth night of the waning moon in late winter. The hunter's tree was a bilva, whose three-part leaves are sacred to Shiva. And under it, hidden in the dark, was a lingam, the simple rounded stone that stands for Shiva in temples and shrines. All night his dropped leaves fell on it, and drops from his water pot spilled on it. He fasted, because he had no food. He stayed awake, because he had to. Without meaning to, he had done what Shivaratri asks: fast, keep vigil, offer water and bilva leaves to the lingam. In the Shiva Purana's telling, deer come to the pool through the night, and each one asks to be spared long enough to go home first, and the hunter, softening, lets them go. By dawn, the story says, his heart is changed, and Shiva's grace reaches him. And here's the teaching devotees love in it. Shiva is called Bholenath, the innocent lord, and Ashutosh, the one quickly pleased. A few leaves, a little water, a night without sleep, given even by accident, reached him. You don't need to be learned to begin; you need to show up. That's why temples stay open until morning, full of people who may know only five syllables. Devotees pour water, milk and honey over the lingam, a rite called abhisheka, and repeat na-mah shi-va-ya, Om Namah Shivaya, bowing to Shiva, until the sky gets light.
screen: `MAHA SHIVARATRI: THE GREAT NIGHT.` · `BILVA LEAVES FALL ON A HIDDEN LINGAM.` · `A FAST AND A VIGIL, BY ACCIDENT.` · `BHOLENATH, ASHUTOSH: QUICKLY PLEASED.` · then, large: `ASHUTOSH: SHIVA IS QUICKLY PLEASED.`

segments.voice: Sit upright, the way the hunter had to on his branch. On each slow breath out, say the five syllables, Om Namah Shivaya, or if you don't pray, simply count the breath. When the first urge comes to stop, to check your phone, to be done, stay for three more breaths. If there's a little water nearby, end the way the hunter did without knowing: pour a few drops onto a plant, as a small offering.
Shivaratri. The night of Shiva, kept with fasting, water and bilva leaves on the lingam, and Om Namah Shivaya until dawn, for the lord who is quickly pleased.
screen: `SHIVARATRI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Ashutosh, Shiva is quickly pleased. The hunter found it by accident. Good night, for now.

676.title: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection
676.hook: a sister ties a thread on her brother's wrist, and he promises to look after her
676.carry: raksha: protecting your people is dharma
676.howItsDone: On the full moon of Shravana, sisters perform a short aarti for their brothers, mark their foreheads, tie a rakhi on the right wrist and feed them a sweet; brothers give a gift and a promise of protection. Many families now include cousins, friends and sisters tying rakhis on sisters.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shivaratri, the night of Shiva, and a hunter who kept it by accident. Your line was Ashutosh, Shiva is quickly pleased. Today, a thread.
screen: `ASHUTOSH: SHIVA IS QUICKLY PLEASED.`

segments.voice: In August, in office lifts and school corridors across India, you'll notice something on boys' and men's wrists: bright threads, some plain red and gold, some with a big foam flower or a cartoon character on them. Some men have six or seven, up to the elbow. Each one was tied by a sister, or a cousin, or a friend who calls him brother. Ask him to take one off and he'll look at you like you asked him to throw away a letter.
screen: `THREADS ON EVERY WRIST.` → `SOME UP TO THE ELBOW.` → `EACH ONE TIED BY A SISTER.`

segments.voice: Raksha means protection. Bandhan means a tie, a binding. Raksha Bandhan: the tie of protection. The thread itself is the rakhi. The festival falls on the full moon of the month of Shravana, in the monsoon. The ritual is short. The sister prepares a small plate: a lamp, a little red powder, a few grains of rice, sweets, the rakhi. She puts a mark on her brother's forehead, waves the lamp before him, and ties the thread on his right wrist. She feeds him a sweet. He gives her a gift, and a promise: to look after her, to stand by her. The best-loved story behind it: Draupadi tore a strip from her sari to bind Krishna's bleeding finger, and Krishna promised to protect her; in that telling, when she is humiliated at the dice game and calls on him, he keeps his word. The story is widely loved, though the torn sari isn't found in the Mahabharata's text itself; it comes from the telling. Now the teaching under the thread. In Hindu thought, protecting the people bound to you isn't a favor. It's dharma, sacred duty. An old Sanskrit saying puts it in three words: dharmo rakshati rakshitah, dharma protects the one who protects it. And in Draupadi's story, even God keeps the promise. Today the festival has stretched. Sisters tie rakhis on sisters, friends on friends, and people mail them across oceans, so a duty made in one city gets worn on a wrist in another.
screen: `RAKSHA: PROTECTION. BANDHAN: A TIE.` · `A MARK, A LAMP, A THREAD, A SWEET.` · `DRAUPADI'S TORN SARI, AS IT'S TOLD.` · `DHARMO RAKSHATI RAKSHITAH.` · then, large: `RAKSHA: PROTECTING YOUR PEOPLE IS DHARMA.`

segments.voice: Rest your left hand lightly around your right wrist, where a rakhi would go, and feel the pulse, or just the warmth. Bring to mind one person you're bound to protect, a sibling, a friend, a child, a neighbor. Let the promise form without words. If you pray, offer it the way Draupadi trusted Krishna; if you don't, simply hold it as a duty you've chosen.
Rakhi. The thread tied on Raksha Bandhan, the tie of protection: a sister's thread, and a brother's promise, kept as dharma.

segments.voice: Your line: raksha, protecting your people is dharma. Tomorrow, the butter thief. Day six hundred seventy-six, done.

677.howItsDone: Many Hindus fast on Janmashtami, sing bhajans, bathe and dress an image of baby Krishna at midnight and rock it in a cradle, then break the fast with milk sweets; many families keep a Laddu Gopal image and care for him daily, and in Maharashtra Dahi Handi teams build human pyramids the next day.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: rakhi, a thread on a brother's wrist and a promise of protection. Your line was raksha, protecting your people is dharma. Today, the midnight birthday again.
screen: `RAKSHA: PROTECTING YOUR PEOPLE IS DHARMA.`

segments.voice: Same birthday, other side of the door: the kitchen. For many Hindu families, Janmashtami isn't only a story told. It's a day cooked, sung and stayed up for. And the morning after, in Maharashtra, young men climb on each other's shoulders, level on level, to reach a clay pot of yogurt hanging over the street.
screen: `THE SAME NIGHT, FROM THE KITCHEN.` → `A DAY COOKED, SUNG, STAYED UP FOR.` → `A HUMAN TOWER AND A POT.`

segments.voice: The day begins with a fast. Some take no food at all, some only fruit and milk, until midnight. A small cradle, a jhula, is set up for baby Krishna, and people sing bhajans, devotional songs. At twelve the conch sounds, and the little image is bathed in milk and honey, dressed in tiny new clothes, and rocked. Only then is the fast broken, often with sweets made of milk and butter. Why butter? Because of the child. In the Bhagavata Purana, Krishna grows up among cowherds in Gokul, and the women come to his mother, Yashoda, to complain: he steals our butter, he feeds it to the monkeys, he breaks the pots. They hang the pots high; he piles up stools and mortars and climbs. Then the same chapter tells something astonishing. The boys report that Krishna has eaten dirt. Yashoda makes him open his mouth, and inside it she sees the whole universe: sky, mountains, oceans, stars, even her own village, and herself. She's shaken. And then, the Bhagavata says, the Lord lets her forget, and she simply picks up her boy and loves him. That's the teaching. Hindus call it vatsalya: loving God the way a parent loves a child. The God who holds every world chose to be scolded, fed and rocked to sleep. It's why many families keep a small image of baby Krishna, Laddu Gopal, and care for him every day: bathe him, dress him, feed him. And it's why, the day after, in Maharashtra, teams called govindas build human towers to break a pot of yogurt, Dahi Handi, cheering for the butter thief.
screen: `THE CRADLE, THE CONCH, THE BATH.` · `MAKHAN CHOR: THE BUTTER THIEF.` · `THE UNIVERSE IN HIS MOUTH.` · then, large: `VATSALYA: LOVING GOD LIKE YOUR OWN CHILD.` · `LADDU GOPAL AND DAHI HANDI.`

segments.voice: Many families tend baby Krishna like a child of the house. For the sit, picture him in his cradle with butter on his hands, or a small child you love. Feel how that love asks nothing back. On each slow breath out, say softly, Gopala, little cowherd, or if you don't pray, just rest in that tenderness. Let it be warm, not solemn.
Janmashtami. Krishna's birthday: a fast, a cradle rocked at midnight, and a God loved like a child, the butter thief.

678.title: Ganesha and the laughing moon
678.hook: the moon laughs at Ganesha's fall, and meets the lord of obstacles
678.carry: the lord of obstacles humbles pride
678.howItsDone: Hindus pray to Ganesha first, before weddings, exams and new beginnings, as the lord of obstacles; on Ganesh Chaturthi some families avoid looking at the moon, and some read or hear the Syamantaka jewel story as a remedy if they see it by accident.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Janmashtami, and the butter thief. Your line was vatsalya, loving God like your own child. Today, a night not to look up.
screen: `VATSALYA: LOVING GOD LIKE YOUR OWN CHILD.`

segments.voice: Here's a strange rule some families keep on Ganesh Chaturthi. With a clay Ganesha just carried home and drums still echoing in the street, a grandmother says: whatever you do tonight, don't look at the moon. Kids who've never heard it immediately want to look. Why not look at the moon on Ganesha's own birthday? Because, people say, Ganesha and the moon once had a very bad evening.
screen: `A CLAY GUEST, JUST ARRIVED.` → `DON'T LOOK AT THE MOON TONIGHT.` → `A VERY BAD EVENING.`

segments.voice: The story, as it's told, goes like this. On his birthday, Ganesha has been offered modak after modak, the sweet dumplings, and he's eaten them all. Late at night, very full, he's riding home on his mouse. A snake crosses the path. The mouse panics, Ganesha tumbles off, and his belly splits, modaks rolling everywhere. Up in the sky, the moon, proud of his beauty, laughs. Ganesha curses the moon: whoever looks at you will be falsely accused. The moon is horrified, and the gods come to plead. Ganesha softens. He doesn't take the curse back completely, but he narrows it to this one night, the fourth day of his month. That's why some families keep their eyes down on Chaturthi night. In some tellings, Krishna glimpses the moon on Chaturthi and is soon accused of stealing a famous jewel, the Syamantaka; the Bhagavata tells how he had to find the jewel to clear his name. People say hearing that story lifts the curse if you looked by accident. Now the teaching. Ganesha is Vighneshvara, the lord of obstacles. Hindus pray to him first, before a wedding, an exam, a new home. But the tradition is honest that he also sets obstacles in the way, especially in front of pride. The moon was the most beautiful thing in the sky, and it laughed. Ganesha put one obstacle in its path, and when the moon was sorry, he softened it. Many teachers read it this way: the bow to Ganesha before anything begins is also a lowering of pride, and the obstacle in front of you is sometimes your own pride. He clears it when you bow.
screen: `TOO MANY MODAKS, ONE SNAKE.` · `THE MOON LAUGHS, AND IS CURSED.` · `KRISHNA AND THE SYAMANTAKA JEWEL.` · `VIGHNESHVARA: LORD OF OBSTACLES.` · then, large: `THE LORD OF OBSTACLES HUMBLES PRIDE.`

segments.voice: Before beginning anything, many Hindus say a short prayer to Ganesha that ends: nirvighnam kuru me deva, Lord, keep my way free of obstacles. Say that line on a few slow breaths out, or if you don't pray, the word clear. Then recall a recent moment when someone laughed at you, or you laughed at someone. Feel the heat of it. On a slow out-breath, bow your head a little, and set most of it down.
Ganesh Chaturthi. Ganesha's fourth day, and the night, people say, not to look at the moon, after the lord of obstacles humbled it, then softened his curse.

segments.voice: Your line: the lord of obstacles humbles pride. And softens, when asked. See you tomorrow.

679.title: One Goddess, nine forms
679.hook: nine nights, nine forms, and a battlefield where the Goddess says there's no one else
679.carry: ekam sat: one truth, many names
679.howItsDone: Many Hindus honor one of the nine forms of Durga, the Navadurga, on each night of Navaratri, with that form's prayers and offerings; some fast all nine days, some wear a set color each day, and many end by honoring young girls as the Goddess on the eighth or ninth day.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ganesha and the laughing moon. Your line was the lord of obstacles humbles pride.
screen: `THE LORD OF OBSTACLES HUMBLES PRIDE.`

segments.voice: Near the shrine in a North Indian home during Navaratri, you may find a small calendar taped up: one name for each night, all the way to nine. Some families wear a different color each day to match. It looks like nine goddesses. Ask the grandmother who keeps the calendar, and she'll likely tell you: it's one Goddess, nine ways.
screen: `A CALENDAR BY THE SHRINE.` → `ONE NAME FOR EACH NIGHT.` → `ONE GODDESS, NINE WAYS.`

segments.voice: The nine forms are the Navadurga, nine Durgas, and in the common list they move through a life: Shailaputri, daughter of the mountain; Brahmacharini, the seeker who fasts in the forest to win Shiva; Chandraghanta and Kushmanda; Skandamata, the mother; Katyayani, the warrior; Kalaratri, the dark night who destroys fear; Mahagauri, radiant and calm; and Siddhidatri, giver of every attainment. Devotees honor one each night, and many fast. So are they nine goddesses? The Devi Mahatmya, the scripture many read aloud through Navaratri, answers with a story. The demon king Shumbha has watched a whole army of goddesses fight beside Durga. Furious, he taunts her: you're proud, but you only win by leaning on other women's strength. And the Goddess answers: I am alone here in the world. Who else is there besides me? These are my own powers, coming back into me. And every goddess on the field disappears into her body, until she stands alone and faces him herself. That's one of Hinduism's oldest and biggest teachings, and the answer to anyone who asks if Hindus have nine goddesses, or a thousand gods. The Rig Veda says it in four words: ekam sat vipra bahudha vadanti. Truth is one; the wise call it by many names. Many forms, one reality. And on the eighth or ninth day, many families invite young girls home, wash their feet, feed them and honor them as the Goddess: one more form she takes.
screen: `NAVADURGA: NINE FORMS.` · `DAUGHTER, SEEKER, MOTHER, WARRIOR, DARK NIGHT, PEACE.` · `WHO ELSE IS THERE BESIDES ME?` · `EVERY GODDESS RETURNS TO HER.` · then, large: `EKAM SAT: ONE TRUTH, MANY NAMES.`

segments.voice: Many families honor one form of the Goddess each night. Pick the one that fits your week: the seeker who doesn't give up, the mother, the warrior, or the dark night who destroys fear. Say her name softly on a few breaths out, then let it rest into one word: Ma, mother. If you don't pray, name the strength you need, then notice it's the same strength under every name.
Navaratri. Nine nights, nine forms, the Navadurga, and one Goddess under every name.
